channel.description: Recent content in Reporting on Best of AI

item.title: Anaplan
item.description:
Anaplan lets large organizations plan in a connected way. Instead of separate spreadsheets for finance, sales, and operations, teams build models on a shared platform so a change in one area, such as a drop in demand, flows through to inventory, headcount, and budget. Its modeling engine handles large multidimensional data, and planners can create scenarios to see the effects of different decisions before committing.

AI features aim to lower the barrier to building and using models. An assistant can help create or modify model logic from natural language, forecast with machine learning, and summarize results for decision-makers. The platform integrates with ERP, CRM, and data warehouse systems to pull in actuals, and offers applications for common planning needs, such as sales territory planning and supply chain optimization.

item.title: BigQuery
item.description: BigQuery lets teams analyze huge amounts of data without managing servers. You load data from files, databases, streams, or other Google services, write SQL, and BigQuery spreads the work across many machines and returns results quickly, whether the table holds millions or trillions of rows. Because storage and compute are separated and managed, there is no cluster to size or tune, which is a big reason analytics teams like it.

item.title: Bloomberg Terminal
item.description: The Bloomberg Terminal is the main workstation for traders, portfolio managers, analysts, and bankers. It delivers real-time and historical prices across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, together with news, research, company data, and analytics. A command-based interface lets users call up functions with short codes, which is why people who use it daily rarely touch menus. Its messaging system, Bloomberg Chat, is also where much of the market does its dealing.

item.title: Deepnote
item.description:
Deepnote reimagines the Jupyter notebook for teams. Several people can edit a notebook at once, comment on cells, and run code on managed cloud machines without setup. It connects to data sources such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Postgres, and supports SQL blocks alongside Python, so analysts can mix queries and analysis.

Results are easy to share. Notebooks can be published as interactive apps or dashboards with inputs, charts can be built without code, and scheduled runs keep outputs fresh. Version history and permissions help with team workflows, and it works with common libraries and Jupyter files.

item.title: FactSet
item.description:
FactSet is one of the main data providers for banks, asset managers, and hedge funds. It aggregates information from many sources into a single platform: company financials, earnings estimates, ownership, supply chain relationships, news, transcripts, and market prices. Analysts use it to screen companies, build models, check ownership, and prepare reports, and portfolio managers use its analytics to measure risk and performance.

Delivery options range from the FactSet Workstation, an interface with analytics and charting, to data feeds and APIs that supply data to a firm’s own systems, and add-ins for Excel. Generative AI features let users search and summarize documents such as earnings calls and filings in natural language, and the company offers tools to connect its data to AI applications and agents. It also provides content for wealth managers and corporate users.

item.title: Heap
item.description:
Heap approaches analytics with automatic capture. Once its snippet is on a site or app, it records user interactions without developers adding tracking code for each event. Product managers can then define what counts as a signup or a purchase later and look back at historical data, which avoids the gaps that come from forgetting to instrument something.

Analysis tools include funnels, retention, user paths, and session replay, and a feature that surfaces friction points and drop-offs. It supports building segments of users and comparing their behavior, and it can send data to a warehouse. Heap was acquired by Contentsquare, which combines its quantitative analytics with Contentsquare’s digital experience tools.

item.title: Kaggle
item.description:
Kaggle is where many data scientists learn and prove their skills. Companies and researchers post competitions with real problems, such as predicting outcomes from data or classifying images, and participants submit models to a leaderboard. Winning solutions are often published, and the discussion forums are a rich source of techniques. Rankings and medals help build a public track record.

The platform offers more than contests. Public datasets cover topics from health to sports, free notebooks run Python and R in the browser with access to GPUs and TPUs within limits, and a models hub shares pretrained models. Kaggle Learn provides short, practical courses on Python, pandas, machine learning, and more. Benchmarks and community challenges around large language models have been added, and the site integrates with Google Cloud.

item.title: Matillion
item.description:
Matillion is a data integration platform. Data teams use a visual designer to extract data from sources, load it into a cloud warehouse, and transform it there using the warehouse’s own compute. This ELT approach scales with the warehouse and keeps data in the company’s environment.

AI has become part of the product through Maia, a set of agents that act as virtual data engineers. A user describes what they need, and Maia can create pipelines, suggest fixes when something fails, and write documentation. Humans stay in the loop and can review the generated work. The platform also supports orchestration, scheduling, and version control with Git.

item.title: Meltano
item.description:
Meltano treats data integration like software development. A project defines extractors and loaders in a configuration file, and Meltano runs them to move data from sources into a warehouse. Because everything is code, pipelines live in Git, run in CI, and can be reviewed like other changes.

It builds on the Singer standard, which has hundreds of community connectors, and integrates with dbt for transformations and Airflow for orchestration. Teams can write custom connectors with a software development kit, which is handy for sources that commercial tools do not cover.

item.title: Mixpanel
item.description:
Mixpanel helps product teams understand behavior. You send events from your product, such as sign-ups, searches, and purchases, along with properties about users, and Mixpanel turns them into reports. Funnels show where people drop off, retention charts show who comes back, flows map the paths people take, and cohorts group users by behavior. Self-serve reports let product managers and marketers answer questions without writing SQL.

The platform includes more than charts. Session replay shows what users actually did, feature flags and experiments test changes, and lexicon tools manage the data schema. AI features let people ask questions in plain language and generate reports, summarize findings, and surface anomalies. Data can be connected from warehouses, and Mixpanel integrates with tools for marketing, support, and customer data pipelines.

item.title: Oracle NetSuite
item.description:
NetSuite was one of the first cloud ERP systems and is widely used by growing companies. A single system runs financials, inventory, procurement, order management, billing, and customer relationship management, so departments work from the same data instead of reconciling spreadsheets. Industry editions adapt it for areas like wholesale distribution, manufacturing, retail, and software, and it supports multiple subsidiaries, currencies, and tax rules, which suits companies expanding internationally.

AI features sit across the suite. Generative tools can summarize records, draft emails and descriptions, and answer questions about data in plain language, while machine learning supports forecasting, anomaly detection, and automation of accounting tasks like matching invoices. Reporting and analytics tools let finance teams build dashboards, and SuiteScript and workflows allow customization.

item.title: Pendo
item.description:
Pendo helps product teams understand and improve their software. After adding a snippet to an application, Pendo records usage automatically: which pages and features people use, where they drop off, and how behavior varies by customer or segment. Product managers use dashboards, funnels, and retention reports to decide what to build and what to fix.

The platform lets teams act on insights without waiting for developers. In-app guides, tooltips, announcements, and checklists guide users through features, surveys and NPS collect feedback, and a roadmap tool captures feature requests. Session replay shows what people did, and AI features summarize feedback, suggest improvements, and analyze conversations with AI features inside products, which is a growing need as software adds assistants.

item.title: Pigment
item.description:
Pigment is a modern take on planning software. Finance teams build models of their company, including headcount, revenue, and spend, in an environment that feels familiar to spreadsheet users but works with large data volumes and multiple dimensions. Plans link across departments, so a hiring plan updates the budget automatically.

It supports scenario planning, which lets teams test the impact of different assumptions side by side, and produces dashboards and reports for executives. AI agents help analyze variances, generate commentary, and build parts of models from prompts. Integrations bring in data from ERP and CRM systems and data warehouses.

item.title: Plausible
item.description:
Plausible keeps analytics simple. A tiny script collects page views, visitors, referrers, devices, and locations without using cookies or storing personal data, so most sites do not need a consent banner for it. The dashboard fits on a single page, which makes it quick to read for people who don’t want to learn a complex tool.

It supports goals and events, so site owners can track signups or purchases, and funnels for conversion steps. Features like UTM tracking and a stats API round out the basics. The code is open source, and users can self-host a free community edition or pay for the hosted service, which is run from European servers.

item.title: Qlik
item.description: Qlik is known for its associative engine, which treats all the data in an app as connected. When you click a value in a chart, everything else updates to show related data, and values that are unrelated are shown as excluded, which helps users discover connections they did not think to query. This differs from tools that require predefined queries and has been a selling point for business users exploring data.

item.title: SAP Concur
item.description:
Concur is a staple of corporate finance. Employees book travel, capture receipts with a phone, and submit expense reports, which flow through approvals and into accounting systems. Policies are applied automatically, flagging out-of-policy spending, and credit card feeds reduce manual entry. Finance teams use it to control costs, reimburse employees, and meet audit requirements.

The platform has grown to include invoice and travel management, with integrations to airlines, hotels, and payment providers. AI supports automatic receipt reading, categorization, audit of expenses to detect errors or fraud, and assistance through SAP’s Joule for answering questions and completing tasks. Reporting provides visibility into travel and spending trends.

item.title: Streamlit
item.description: Streamlit is built for data scientists who want to share work without learning web development. You write a Python script and add calls like text input, sliders, charts, and buttons, and Streamlit produces an interactive web app that reruns the script when the user changes something. This model is simple enough that people can make an app in minutes, and it has become a standard for internal tools and demos.

item.title: YNAB
item.description:
YNAB is as much a method as an app. Users assign each dollar of income to a category, such as rent, groceries, or savings, and update the plan as real spending happens. When money moves between categories, the app shows the tradeoff. The idea is to work from money you already have, not money you expect, which many people find reduces financial stress.

Features support that approach. Bank syncing imports transactions, goals track bills and savings targets, reports show spending trends, and shared budgets let partners manage money together. The company offers workshops and guides that teach the approach, which is a big part of why users stick with it. There is a mobile app and a web version.

item.title: Blend
item.description:
Blend builds software for lenders. Instead of paper forms and email, borrowers apply on a digital platform that collects information, connects to bank accounts and payroll sources to verify income and assets, and tracks the status of the application. Loan officers and processors see the file in a shared workflow.

Automation cuts the manual work in underwriting preparation. The platform pulls data from verified sources, checks documents, and flags missing or inconsistent items so staff can fix problems early. It covers mortgages, home equity, and consumer lending products, and integrates with loan origination systems and credit providers.

item.title: Daloopa
item.description:
Daloopa serves the finance professionals who build models from public company reports. Instead of typing numbers from filings into Excel, an analyst gets a database of financial line items pulled from documents like quarterly reports and presentations, with each number linked back to its source in the original file.

Updates arrive soon after companies report, so models stay current. An Excel add-in lets analysts pull data into their own templates, and an API and integrations with AI assistants allow data to flow into other workflows. The company has focused on accuracy and traceability, since errors in financial data are costly.

item.title: Floify
item.description:
Floify handles the document stage of mortgage lending. Loan officers invite borrowers to a secure portal where they upload pay stubs, bank statements, and other items, sign disclosures electronically, and watch the status of their loan. The portal carries the lender’s branding.

Automation reduces manual follow-up. The system sends reminders for missing documents, sorts and labels uploads, and updates borrowers and real estate agents as milestones are reached. It connects to loan origination systems so data moves between them. Analytics show where loans get stuck.

item.title: nCino
item.description:
nCino is cloud banking software. A bank uses it to manage the full lending process, from application to documents, analysis, approval, and closing, replacing paper and email chains. It covers commercial, consumer, and mortgage lending and account opening.

AI and automation reduce manual work. Models extract financial data from documents, assess credit risk, and flag items for review, and agents help with tasks like drafting credit memos. Dashboards give management visibility across the portfolio.

item.title: Rogo
item.description:
Rogo focuses on the work of junior bankers and analysts, who spend hours digging through filings, transcripts, and data. A user asks a question in plain language, such as how a company’s margins compare with peers, and Rogo retrieves and analyzes the sources, citing where numbers came from.

It connects to financial data providers and a firm’s internal documents, produces outputs like comps and summaries, and fits into the workflow with tools such as Excel and PowerPoint. Security and compliance features suit regulated firms.

item.title: Sales Boomerang
item.description:
Sales Boomerang helps brokers stay in touch at the right time. It connects to a broker’s client list, watches for signals such as changes in credit, equity, or market rates, and alerts the broker when a former client might benefit from refinancing or a new purchase.

That turns a dormant database into leads. Automated outreach can follow, with messages personalized to the situation. Brokers use it to generate repeat and referral business without constant manual review.

item.title: QueryStory
item.description:
QueryStory approaches analytics with agents. A team connects its data sources and describes the business, such as its metrics and definitions, and then asks questions in natural language. The agents write queries, analyze results, and respond with explanations and visuals.

The point is to go beyond a static chart. When a number moves, a user can ask why, and the agent investigates by looking at breakdowns and related data. Business context helps the agent interpret questions the way an analyst on the team would.

item.title: Dataiku
item.description:
Dataiku aims to let analysts, data scientists, and engineers work in the same environment. Teams connect to data sources, clean and prepare data with visual recipes or code, build models, and deploy them as applications or services. The visual interface lowers the barrier for business users, while coders can use notebooks and libraries.

The platform has added tools for generative AI, including connecting to language models, building retrieval applications, and creating agents. Governance features track models and projects, assess risk, and document decisions, which large organizations need to meet internal and regulatory requirements.

item.title: SwiftAlerts
item.description:
SwiftAlerts gathers market data into a structure that agents can query. Instead of hunting through separate sources, an agent can ask about relationships between trades, holdings, filings, and sentiment, and get connected answers.

The idea fits the rise of AI agents that research and monitor markets. Reliable data is essential, since trading decisions on wrong information lose money, and nothing from such a tool is financial advice.

Independent information is limited, so check data sources, update speed, and terms. SwiftAlerts is free to start. Alternatives include Unusual Whales, Quiver Quantitative, Benzinga, Polygon.io, and Financial Datasets. SwiftAlerts suits developers building market agents, with caution.

item.title: Anomaly AI
item.description:
Anomaly AI is for people who work with data that is too big or messy for a normal spreadsheet. A user uploads Excel or CSV files or connects sources such as databases, warehouses, and Google Sheets, then asks questions in natural language. The tool answers with tables, charts, and written explanations.

The vendor emphasizes traceable answers, meaning the analysis is run as code against the data so results can be inspected and not just generated by a language model. It can merge files with database data in one analysis, find trends, and flag unusual values. A connector allows assistants like Claude to hand questions about your data to the service.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: Hex
item.description:
Hex combines notebooks with business intelligence. Teams connect their data warehouse, write SQL and Python in a notebook, and turn the results into interactive apps that non-technical colleagues can use without code. Everything lives in one place with version history and comments.

AI is built into the workflow. Magic helps write and fix queries and code, and agents let business users ask questions of governed data in plain language. A semantic layer keeps definitions of metrics consistent, so answers match across reports. Scheduled runs keep outputs fresh.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: Snowflake
item.description:
Snowflake pioneered the cloud data warehouse built on this separation. Companies load data, run SQL queries with elastic compute, and share datasets securely with partners. It runs on the major clouds, and teams of analysts and engineers use it as a central data foundation.

The platform has grown into an AI data cloud. Cortex provides language model functions, search over documents, and agents that run inside the platform, close to the data, with governance. It also supports machine learning, Python workloads, and apps built on Snowflake data.

item.title: Looker
item.description:
Looker takes a modeling-first approach. Data teams define dimensions and measures in LookML, a code-based language, and users explore data and build dashboards on top of those shared definitions. This keeps numbers consistent and cuts arguments over whose revenue figure is right.

The platform queries data warehouses directly, so it works with the company’s data without extracting it. It supports embedded analytics, letting companies put dashboards in their own products. Gemini in Looker adds conversational analytics and help writing LookML and building reports.

item.title: Wealth.com
item.description:
Wealth.com brings estate planning into the advisory relationship. Advisors can generate estate documents for clients through guided workflows, with attorney review options, and offer a client portal that shows the plan visually. A vault stores documents.

AI reads existing estate documents and summarizes provisions, beneficiaries, and issues, which helps advisors understand a client’s situation quickly. The platform integrates with financial planning tools so estate information sits alongside the rest of the plan.

item.title: Airbyte
item.description: Airbyte solves the data movement problem. Data teams use it to pull information from applications, databases, and APIs, such as Salesforce, Postgres, Stripe, and Google Ads, and load it into destinations such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks, on a schedule. Hundreds of pre-built connectors cover common sources, and a low-code builder, with AI assistance, lets teams create connectors for others. Because it is open source, the connector catalog grows with community contributions.

item.title: AlphaSense
item.description: AlphaSense is a search engine for business information. Analysts, investors, and strategy teams use it to find what companies and experts are saying across a large body of documents: earnings call transcripts, SEC filings, broker and industry research, press releases, news, and expert call transcripts. Its search understands financial language, so a query for supply chain risk or pricing pressure returns relevant passages instead of just keyword matches, with highlights and context.

item.title: Amplitude AI
item.description: Amplitude helps product teams see what users actually do. You instrument your app or website to send events, such as signing up, clicking a button, or finishing a purchase, and Amplitude turns them into funnels, retention curves, user paths, and cohorts. These views answer questions like where new users drop off and which features bring people back. It is used by product managers, designers, and data analysts at companies from startups to large enterprises.

item.title: BILL AI
item.description:
BILL helps businesses handle bills and payments without paper and manual entry. Vendors’ invoices arrive by email or upload, the system extracts the details, routes them for approval, and schedules payment by ACH, check, or card. On the receivables side, it sends invoices to customers and collects payments.

AI takes on the data entry. It reads invoice fields, suggests accounting categories, matches invoices to purchase orders and receipts, and flags duplicates or unusual items. Integrations with QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, and other accounting systems keep the books in sync, and spend management tools add corporate cards and expense tracking.

item.title: Botkeeper
item.description:
Botkeeper offered accounting firms a way to scale bookkeeping with automation. Its software connected to clients’ accounting systems, categorized transactions with machine learning, reconciled accounts, and prepared financial statements, with human reviewers checking the work. The aim was to let firms serve more clients with the same staff and to reduce routine data entry.

The company raised substantial funding, but it shut down after losing a large share of its revenue when major customers were acquired and changed their arrangements. It then sold its Infinite AI platform to Xendoo, a bookkeeping firm, which said it would keep the platform active and supported as its own division. The long-term roadmap is less clear, and customers had to decide whether to move.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: Expensify
item.description:
Expensify is known for making expense reports less painful. Employees photograph receipts or forward them by email, SmartScan extracts the merchant, date, and amount, and the app builds a report for submission. Managers approve in the app, and approved expenses sync to accounting software.

Other features cover company spending. The Expensify Card gives employees corporate cards with real-time receipts matching, policies flag out-of-bounds expenses automatically, and mileage tracking and per diems handle travel. AI helps categorize spending and spot policy issues.

item.title: Fivetran
item.description:
Fivetran handles the extract and load steps of data pipelines. A team connects sources such as SaaS applications, databases, and files, picks a destination warehouse, and Fivetran keeps the data synced, adapting automatically when source schemas change. This saves engineers from building and maintaining custom connectors.

The company merged with dbt Labs, the maker of the popular transformation tool, bringing loading and transformation together under one roof. Related products include a metadata and governance layer, and tools that prepare data for AI agents. Features for monitoring, anomaly detection, and lineage help teams trust their data.

item.title: H2O.ai
item.description:
H2O.ai built its reputation on open-source machine learning. H2O-3 is a widely used library for training models on large datasets, with an AutoML feature that tries many algorithms and picks the best. The company’s commercial Driverless AI automated feature engineering and model building for business users, and its tools have been used in finance, insurance, and healthcare.

More recently, H2O.ai has focused on generative AI. H2O LLM Studio lets teams fine-tune language models without much code, h2oGPT is an open-source project for chatting with documents, and its enterprise platform lets companies deploy private assistants and agents, including on-premises or in air-gapped environments. It has also released small language models designed to run efficiently.

item.title: Kensho
item.description:
Kensho began as a startup applying machine learning to financial markets and was acquired by S&P Global, where it operates as the company’s AI innovation hub. Its products address practical data problems in finance. Kensho Link matches records between data sets, such as linking company names across different sources, Kensho Classify tags documents by category, and Kensho Extract pulls data out of PDFs and filings.

More recent work connects financial data to generative AI. Kensho develops tools that allow AI assistants and agents to access S&P Global’s data reliably, with grounding that provides sources for answers, plus language models and benchmarks for finance. Its technology supports S&P products and is available to clients who want to build their own applications.

item.title: Metabase
item.description:
Metabase makes data approachable. Connected to a database or warehouse, it lets non-technical users build questions by clicking through filters and summaries, view results as charts, and assemble dashboards. Analysts can write SQL when they need it, and everything is shareable.

The AI assistant lets users describe what they want, and generates the query or chart, which helps people who do not know the data model. Embedded analytics lets companies place dashboards in their own products. Permissions and models keep data governed.

item.title: Morningstar AI
item.description:
Morningstar is known for independent research on funds, stocks, and markets. Its star ratings for mutual funds and ETFs became a standard reference, and analysts publish research and fair value estimates on companies. Individual investors use its website and premium subscriptions to screen investments and build portfolios, while advisors and institutions use products like Morningstar Direct for deeper analysis, portfolio construction, and reporting.

AI has been added to make research easier to navigate. Mo is a conversational assistant that answers investing questions using Morningstar’s research and data, summarizes reports, and explains concepts, with an emphasis on drawing from the company’s own vetted content to limit errors. Other uses include automated summaries of earnings calls and analyst notes, and data tools that help build screens and analyze holdings.

item.title: Mosaic
item.description:
Mosaic is aimed at finance teams that want a modern view of the business. It pulls data from accounting systems, sales tools, and HR platforms into a single model, so metrics like revenue, headcount, and cash are current and consistent. Teams build reports and board decks from live data.

Forecasting and scenario tools let teams test assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing changes, and see the impact. AI allows users to ask questions in plain language and get analysis, and automates routine commentary and variance explanations.

item.title: Pilot
item.description:
Pilot offers accounting as a service. A company connects its bank accounts and tools, and Pilot’s team and software keep the books, close each month, prepare financial statements, and handle tax filings. Clients get a dedicated bookkeeper and a dashboard.

Automation takes on the repetitive work, such as categorizing transactions, while humans check results and answer questions. Add-on services include CFO advice, R&D tax credits, and sales tax support.

Pilot is priced by monthly fee based on complexity, and aimed at startups and small to mid-sized businesses. It is a service, not self-serve software. Alternatives include Bench (which shut down and was acquired by Employer.com), Puzzle, Digits, Xero with an accountant, and QuickBooks Live. Pilot suits startups that want outsourced accounting.

item.title: PitchBook
item.description:
PitchBook tracks private markets. Its database covers companies, funding rounds, investors, funds, acquisitions, and valuations, and analysts use it to find targets, benchmark deals, and research sectors. Reports and data feeds support investment decisions and strategy work.

AI tools help users query the database in natural language, summarize companies and markets, and speed up research tasks. Integrations with Excel and CRM systems bring data into daily workflows. The company also publishes market research.

item.title: Plaid
item.description: Plaid connects apps to bank accounts. When you link an account in a budgeting app, investment platform, or payments service, Plaid’s interface asks you to sign in to your bank, and the app then receives only the data you permit. Developers use Plaid’s APIs to verify account ownership, check balances, read transaction history, confirm identity, assess income and assets for lending, and initiate transfers, without building separate integrations with thousands of banks.

item.title: PostHog AI
item.description:
PostHog bundles the tools product teams use to understand and improve their software. After adding its SDK, you can track events, build funnels and retention charts, watch session recordings, run experiments, release features gradually with flags, collect feedback through surveys, and analyze data with SQL. Having these in one product, with a shared data set, avoids the cost and complexity of stitching several tools together.

AI features include an assistant that can answer questions about your data, write queries, create charts, and summarize insights in plain language, and tools for monitoring AI applications such as tracing model calls and costs. Because PostHog is open source, it can be self-hosted for data control, or used through PostHog Cloud, and a pipeline can send data to other destinations.

item.title: Power BI
item.description: Power BI turns raw data into visual reports. You connect to sources such as Excel files, SQL databases, cloud services, and Microsoft Fabric, shape the data, define relationships and calculations, and build dashboards with charts, maps, and slicers. Reports can be published to the Power BI service, shared with colleagues, refreshed on a schedule, and embedded in other applications. Because it fits neatly with Excel, Teams, SharePoint, and Azure, it is the default BI tool for many Microsoft-centered companies.

item.title: Scale AI
item.description:
Scale AI built its business on a simple observation: AI models need huge amounts of well-labeled data, and quality control at scale is hard. It combines software with a large network of human contributors and experts to annotate images, video, text, and sensor data. Early customers included self-driving car developers, and the company grew by supplying training data to the biggest AI labs.

Today much of its work involves large language models. Scale provides human feedback data used in reinforcement learning, expert-written examples for fine-tuning, and evaluations that test models for accuracy and safety. Its tools help companies manage data pipelines, and a generative AI platform lets enterprises customize models on their own data. Public-sector work includes AI systems for defense and government agencies, and the company runs public leaderboards that rank models on hard tests.

item.title: Sisense
item.description:
Sisense helps organizations analyze data and share insights. Analysts connect data sources, build models and dashboards, and users explore results in a browser. Its strength is embedding: software companies place Sisense charts and analytics inside their products for customers.

AI features include asking questions in plain language, forecasting, and automatic detection of unusual patterns, plus a generative assistant that builds dashboards. The platform works with cloud data warehouses and offers an API-first approach.

item.title: Stampli
item.description:
Stampli keeps the conversation about an invoice attached to the invoice. When a bill arrives, teams discuss it in context, approvers sign off, and the payment goes out, with no hunting through email threads. It connects to accounting systems and does not require replacing them.

Billy the Bot reads invoices, suggests coding and approvals based on past behavior, and flags anomalies. Payment tools handle payments and cards, and the platform provides audit trails and reporting.

item.title: Tableau
item.description:
Tableau is known for making data exploration feel visual and quick. Analysts connect to databases, spreadsheets, and cloud data warehouses, then drag fields onto a canvas to build charts, maps, and dashboards without writing code. It handles large data volumes well, and its interactivity lets viewers filter, drill down, and compare in ways static reports cannot. It is widely used in finance, healthcare, retail, government, and education.

Salesforce owns Tableau and has built AI into it. Tableau Pulse sends personalized, plain-language insights about key metrics to the people who care about them, and flags unusual changes without anyone opening a dashboard. Tableau Agent helps users build visualizations and analyze data by chatting with the tool. Tableau Prep cleans and combines data, and the platform integrates with Salesforce data and its Data Cloud.

item.title: ThoughtSpot
item.description:
ThoughtSpot built its product around search. Instead of building reports by dragging fields, business users type a question such as sales by region last quarter, and ThoughtSpot generates the right chart from the connected data warehouse, with the ability to drill down and refine. This lowers the barrier for people who are not analysts and reduces the queue of requests for data teams.

Generative AI has expanded the approach. Spotter acts as an AI analyst that understands questions in conversation, runs analyses, explains results, and proposes follow-up questions, while agents can answer questions inside other tools. Liveboards combine charts into shareable dashboards that update from live data, and an embedded analytics offering lets companies put these capabilities in their own products.

item.title: Tipalti
item.description:
Tipalti automates accounts payable for growing companies. Suppliers and partners onboard through a portal that collects tax forms and payment details, invoices are captured and approved, and Tipalti pays them in the local currency and method across many countries.

Compliance is a main benefit: the platform handles tax documentation, sanctions screening, and reporting, which is hard for companies paying people worldwide. AI reads invoices, flags anomalies, and helps reconcile payments in accounting systems.

item.title: Yodlee
item.description:
Yodlee lets financial apps pull in customers’ account data. A budgeting tool, lender, or wealth platform can use Yodlee’s APIs to link to thousands of financial institutions, retrieve balances and transactions, and keep them updated. That saves each company from building separate connections to every bank.

Beyond raw data, Yodlee enriches transactions. Machine learning cleans merchant names, assigns categories, and flags patterns, and analytics products use aggregated data to describe consumer spending trends. Account verification and income checks help lenders confirm information, and the company supports open banking rules in regions where they exist.

item.title: Zeni
item.description:
Zeni provides outsourced finance for startups. Companies connect their bank accounts, and Zeni handles bookkeeping, accounts payable, tax, and CFO services, with a dashboard showing cash, burn, and runway in real time. Humans check the AI’s work.

The service replaces a part-time accountant or finance hire for early-stage companies. Monthly reports help founders and investors understand the business.

Zeni is a subscription service. Alternatives include Pilot, Bench, Puzzle, Digits, and a traditional accountant. Zeni suits startups wanting outsourced finance.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: Monarch Money
item.description:
Monarch Money brings accounts into one dashboard. Users link banks, cards, loans, and investments, and the app tracks spending, net worth, and recurring bills. Budgets can follow a flexible or category-based model, and goals help save toward targets.

Couples and families can share views and manage budgets together while keeping some accounts private. AI categorizes transactions, spots subscriptions, and gives summaries and insights, and an assistant answers questions about finances. Reports show trends over time.

item.title: Trullion
item.description:
Trullion tackles accounting standards that require reading contracts. For leases and revenue contracts, finance teams must pull terms such as payments, dates, and options into calculations. Trullion’s AI reads documents, extracts the data, and generates the schedules and journal entries.

Each figure links back to its source in the document, which helps auditors verify. The platform integrates with accounting systems and handles changes such as lease modifications. It is used by finance teams and audit firms.

item.title: Vic.ai
item.description:
Vic.ai reads invoices and processes them with little manual input. It extracts data, suggests coding to the correct accounts, routes approvals, and flags unusual items, learning from how accountants correct it. The aim is touchless processing for routine invoices.

It integrates with ERP systems such as NetSuite, SAP, and Microsoft Dynamics, and offers payment and analytics features. Accounting firms and mid-sized to large finance teams use it to cut manual work.

item.title: Evalyze
item.description:
Evalyze aims to make fundraising more systematic. A founder uploads a pitch deck, and the tool reviews it for clarity, story, and typical investor concerns, then suggests improvements. It also helps identify investors whose focus matches the company’s stage and sector.

For first-time founders, structured feedback is useful because many lack access to experienced advisors. Matching tools can narrow a long list of investors to those most likely to be interested, which saves time on outreach.

item.title: GoAI
item.description:
GoAI aims to give individual investors some of the research help professionals have. A user searches a company or asks a question, and the tool pulls financial data, summarizes earnings calls and filings, and highlights notable insider trades. Answers are written in plain language to be readable for non-experts.

Such tools save time reading long documents, but they do not predict the market. AI summaries can contain errors, so important figures should be checked against filings. Past results do not guarantee future performance, and nothing a tool generates should be treated as a recommendation.

item.title: Julius AI
item.description: Julius lets people explore data by asking questions. After uploading a CSV or Excel file, or connecting to a database or Google Sheets, you can ask for things like the average sales by region, a trend over time, or a correlation between two columns. Julius writes and runs code behind the scenes, then shows the result as a chart, a table, or a written explanation, and you can view the code to check what it did.

item.title: Jupid
item.description:
Jupid is accounting help for sole proprietors. Users link their bank accounts and cards, and the app sorts each transaction into the categories used on Schedule C, which is the tax form for self-employment income. It flags business expenses, helps separate personal spending, and keeps a running view of profit.

The tool estimates quarterly taxes and highlights deductions that people often miss, which reduces the scramble at tax time. Reports can be exported to share with an accountant or to use when filing. AI handles the sorting and learns from corrections.

item.title: MarketAlerts.ai
item.description:
MarketAlerts.ai watches the market on behalf of its users. Investors list their holdings, and the service monitors news, filings, price moves, and other events, sending alerts when something relevant happens and summarizing why it might matter. Some alerts include AI-generated signals about possible actions.

Such tools save time for people who cannot follow the market all day, but they carry risks. AI-generated trade signals are not reliable predictions, markets are unpredictable, and acting on automated signals can lose money. Nothing here is financial advice.

item.title: Obviously AI
item.description:
Obviously AI was built to make machine learning accessible to business users. You upload a CSV or connect a data source, choose the thing you want to predict, such as customer churn, sales, or lead conversion, and the platform tests multiple algorithms, picks the best one, and shows the results in plain language. It highlights which columns most influence the prediction and lets you try what-if scenarios.

Predictions can be exported or sent to other tools, and the platform offers dashboards for sharing insights with teammates. It positions itself for marketing, sales, finance, and operations analysts who have data but no data scientists, and for consultants who need quick models for clients.

item.title: Page Pulse
item.description:
Page Pulse aims to make analytics approachable. A site owner adds a snippet and sees visitors, popular pages, sources, and conversions in a clear dashboard, without needing to learn a complex reporting interface. The focus is on answers to basic questions about what is working.

Typical users are small businesses, bloggers, and agencies that report to clients and want simple summaries. Some AI features explain trends in plain language and suggest improvements.

item.title: Ramp
item.description:
Ramp issues corporate cards and wraps them in software for controlling spending. Companies give employees physical and virtual cards with limits and rules, and receipts are captured and matched automatically through the app. Finance teams see spending in real time and avoid chasing employees for expense reports. Ramp is known for fast growth among startups and mid-sized businesses.

The product has widened into a finance operating system. Bill pay handles vendor invoices, procurement tools manage purchase requests and approvals, and accounting automation categorizes transactions and syncs with systems such as NetSuite, QuickBooks, and Xero. AI agents review expenses against policy, suggest ways to cut costs from vendor spending data, and handle routine tasks such as coding transactions and preparing month-end close.
